Infectious diseases In the past decades, several emerging and re-emerging infectious diseases have been seen to spread to many parts of the world, causing deaths and sizable burden to the public health system locally and globally.

With public health advancement in areas including vaccination and antibiotics, and overall improvement of living conditions across the world, prevention and treatment of infectious disease have improved globally, especially in high-income countries (6), despite the more frequent recent outbreaks caused by emerging and re-emerging viruses.
Overall, the burden of disease has been shifting from communicable disease to non-communicable diseases (7).
In the Southeast Asia region, where the majority of countries are less developed (8), however, infectious diseases still pose a high disease burden (9).

A national surveillance and response system that aims to detect and respond in a timely manner to infectious disease outbreaks is essential to keep infectious diseases under control at a national level (11).

Endemic infectious diseases can be seasonal in temperate countries, because pathogens only survive and transmit under certain climatic conditions, and people as hosts have different behaviour and contact pattern at different times of the year (15,16).
Regionally, many communicable diseases stay endemic in this region, including some vaccine-preventable diseases, such as diphtheria, measles and pertussis (18).
As a result, regional countries now face new challenges in endemic infectious disease control and prevention (21).

While the response to endemic diseases may be less urgent, the burden caused by pathogens such as influenza and malaria, which are endemic in the region, is high (22–24), and due to their endemicity, many countries have long standing surveillance systems to track outbreaks and guide response, from vector control to hospital bed utilisation (25–27).

Abstract Dengue imposes a substantial burden on health in tropical and subtropical areas and the recent expansion of its range makes it of considerable public health concern worldwide.
Explanations, especially climatic, have been identified to understand the timing of large dengue outbreaks and thereby predict future outbreaks to inform control.
In the city state of Singapore, like other equatorial countries, seasonality is indistinct and thus ostensibly chaotic dengue epidemics occur.
We assessed whether a simple statistical model–with no additional seasonal forcing–is sufficient to capture the patterns of epidemic magnitude and period in Singapore.

Observed dengue time series from 2003 to 2012 was fitted using a simple autoregressive model, and the fitted model was used to simulate synthetic datasets that are governed purely by randomness and short-term contagion but no other drivers.
Here we show through a series of tests that the apparent pattern of epidemics and endemics of dengue in the city state are indistinguishable from chance.

These tests were inspired by the sports randomness study but adapted to the context of dengue time series, including comparing the autocorrelation function, the cumulative probabilities, the conditional probability of a rise, the yearly number of cases, the maximum weekly number of cases over 10 years, and the number of runs.
These novel tests showed that the observed dengue time series was no different from the simulated thousands of time series driven by only chance and contagion but no other drivers.

This implies that public policy makers in Singapore, and by extension other equatorial countries, need to lessen their dependence on explanations of dengue outbreaks, and accept the role of chance therein.

These in turn cause increasing challenges for public health systems, including the increasing burden of infectious disease, and the need to build a surveillance and response system that is able to identify newly emerging disease rapidly, both regionally and internationally which calls for international collaboration, and need for drug and vaccine research and production (112–114).

The optimal balance between model accuracy and complexity is typically obtained through cross-validation: repeatedly partitioning the data into training and validation sets, varying the degree of penalty, optimizing the regression parameters for each penalty value, then selecting the penalty that minimizes out of sample predictive accuracy.

Computationally efficient methods to explore the penalty and parameter space exist (136), making it feasible to use LASSO as part of a ‘real-time’ forecasting pipeline for routinely collected health data such as infectious disease notifications.

While various methods have been proposed in the literature for the forecast of infectious diseases, there has not been any systematic study on a general approach which is applicable with modifications to various diseases in countries with different climatic patterns.

In particular, we assess for diseases with different transmission modalities, in different climatic zones, how accurate short to medium time forecasts can be, and what data streams are necessary for accurate forecasts.
We apply the method to four countries from different latitudes—Japan, Taiwan, Thailand and Singapore—to cover temperate, sub-tropical and tropical settings.

Statistical analysis Wavelet analyses were done to explore periodicity of all endemic diseases and climatic variables in four countries.

As incidence data were generally right skewed and with increased stochasticity during epidemics, we controlled for skewness and heteroscedasticity by log-transforming (after adding one to) the observed number of cases for all analyses, or mean number of cases per sentinel for Japan.
To allow for contagion and typical epidemic duration, we used past incidence of up to a half year (26 weeks for Japan, Taiwan and Singapore; 6 months for Thailand) as autocovariates.

We accommodated nonlinearities in the relationship between past and future incidence by using the quadratic of past incidence (again, up to one half year in the past) as a potential covariate; the inclusion of additional polynomial terms did not improve the results and hence were omitted.
We used climatic variables (minimum, maximum and average temperature, humidity and rainfall) of up to 4 weeks (one month for Thailand).
Wavelet transformations of the covariates and outcomes were not used, to ensure that only data available at the time of the forecast were used to make the forecast.

For each forecast window (from 𝑘𝑘 = 1 time unit to 6, for Thailand (the data being monthly) or 26, for Japan, Taiwan and Singapore (weekly)), a separate LASSO model was developed which used data available at the time of the forecast only.
Ten-fold cross validation was carried out by partitioning the total data set into 10 approximately equal-sized subsamples.

Each subsample was used in turn as the validation set while the rest were used as the training set, the performance was measured through the mean squared error (of the difference between the forecast and the data) on each validation set and averaged over the ten folds.
The constraint (or equivalently, penalty term) that optimized the out of sample performance was then used to refit the model and make projections.

Characterizing the transmission dynamics of A key question is then, how we can characterize the transmission dynamics of vector-borne diseases, such as dengue.

Mathematical and statistical modelling tools are helpful in this respect, as they can exploit the information collected over space and time from surveillance mechanism and inform policy makers on risk factors for vector-borne disease transmission, whether current interventions in place are effective and whether a ramp-up in vector control measures is needed.
Three broad classes of modelling tools were broadly defined by Siettos and Russo [71].
The next category includes mathematical-mechanistic state-space models, including the SIR model and network based models [72].

These can include stochastic assumptions on parameters and also crucially an observation equation for observed disease data, which then allows state-space models to be viewed as a special case of the regression model (due to state equation restrictions).
In terms of vector-borne diseases, these tools effectively provide a means to perform computer experiments where it is not ethical or practical in the real world.

Dimensionless, but important epidemiological quantities such as the effective reproduction number, static reproduction number and force of infection can then be post-hoc inferred for these scenarios under certain classes of models which allows policy makers to understand the long-term implications of vector-borne disease burdens from risk factors.

Forecasts of infectious disease can also be generated from a large suite of mathematical and statistical tools for resource planning and healthcare management purposes and have been well-explored in the literature.

Some examples include the use of conventional time series models such as the autoregressive model with covariates to forecast dengue case counts [76], count process models for severe dengue case counts and/or deaths counts [77], forecast combinations of models incorporating both time-series and mechanistic tools [78] and machine learning frameworks which induce sparsity in the observation equation [46].
While modelling the observation process is well-studied, key gaps still remain in modelling vector-borne diseases in general.

While it may be easier for diseases with strong seasonality, such as influenza in temperate climates, where there are clearly defined periods with elevated case counts [79, 80], for vector-borne diseases which are hyper-endemic, such as dengue in Southeast Asia, reported case counts may always be non-zero and outbreak seasons are less clearly defined.

Global burden Globally, an estimated 105 (95% CI: 95—114) million dengue infections occur each year, of which over half are concentrated in South and Southeast Asia [6].

Aims of thesis Although significant progress has been made in understanding the epidemiology and ecology of Aedes-borne diseases as well as developing new vector control tools and vaccines, a lot of critical knowledge gaps still remain.
In particular, little is known about the true geographical extent of ZIKV, which is believed to be still circulating in many locations in the tropics and subtropics without being detected.
The identification of these locations has important implications for the enhancement of global Zika outbreak preparedness and response capacity.
To achieve this, however, requires knowledge about the geographical areas that should be prioritized for ZIKV surveillance strengthening.
It is hoped that this work will provide valuable evidence to guide the allocation of finite public health resources to mitigate the risk of another large-scale Zika outbreak in the future.

In addition, it remains unclear to what extent weather influences the temporal fluctuation of Aedes abundance inside and nearby residential zones in cities with a tropical climate such as Singapore, although vector control is typically intensified during the wet season.
The results generated from this study can be used to guide the refinement of Aedes control strategies in Singapore.
Furthermore, few studies, if any, have been conducted to identify the main drivers for the variation in vector control effectiveness across different dengue endemic settings.
It is hoped that this work will generate useful insights to guide the development of Aedes control strategic plans to achieve sustained reduction in the burden of dengue.
The identification of locations with potential and unknown spread of ZIKV is a key yet understudied component for outbreak preparedness.

Here, we aim to identify locations at a high risk of cryptic ZIKV spread during 2015–2016 to further the understanding of the global ZIKV epidemiology, which is critical for the mitigation of the risk of future epidemics.
Thereafter, a global risk model was applied to estimate the weekly ZIKV transmissibility during 2015–2016 for each location.
Finally, we assessed the risk of onward ZIKV spread following importation in each susceptible spatial unit to identify locations with a high potential for cryptic ZIKV spread during 2015–2016.

Conclusion Our study has provided valuable insights into the potentially high-risk locations for cryptic ZIKV circulation during the 2015–2016 pandemic and has also laid a foundation for future studies that attempt to further narrow this key knowledge gap.

Elsewhere, a cross-sectional study conducted between November 2015 and June 2016 in Kinshasa, Democratic Republic of Congo, found that 30.2% and 26.4% of the participants had experienced past dengue and Chikungunya infections respectively [200].

Our study must be interpreted in light of the following limitations.

For each susceptible spatial unit, we were unable to quantify the population-level immunity immediately prior to the 2015–2016 global ZIKV epidemic, largely owing to the paucity of updated serological data, which also include antibody titre data that are needed to account for the effect of pre-existing dengue immunity on the susceptibility to ZIKV infection in each location [220].

In addition, we did not account for land or sea transport in our analysis, and assumed their impact on our estimates to be limited given that most ZIKV infections that were imported from donor to susceptible spatial units involved air travel, although short-range commuting flows could play a more important role in the epidemic invasion path once the virus was introduced to a new country or continent [222].

We also did not consider importation caused by infected passengers in transit who entered a country as short-term visitors before reaching their final destinations, due to the generally short LOS presumed for these relatively small number of individuals.

Besides, our study did not account for the impact of weather variables such as rainfall on the seasonal variation in vector-to-host ratios, which is challenging to model on a global scale and can be further explored in future work.

In other words, it is not possible to reveal all the locations at a high risk of cryptic ZIKV spread in a single modelling study, and the findings generated in this study were conditional on the currently available data only.
Conclusion In conclusion, our study has provided valuable insights into the potentially high-risk locations for cryptic ZIKV circulation during the 2015–2016 pandemic.

text: The implementation of social distancing measures in Singapore has been progressive from 10 March with the rollout of gradually stricter recommendations and regulations, leading to the implementation of a 'circuit breaker', or lockdown, on 7 April 2020 in response to rising autochthonous cases.
source: Dickens et al. (Cook AR senior author) · Lancet Regional Health Western Pacific 2020 · PMC7395828

text: Although Singapore's lockdown seemingly had no effect on several large outbreaks among foreign worker dormitories that started in early April, it appears to have arrested the epidemic growth in the general population, using school closures and workplace distancing as recognized and effective attack rate reduction measures.
source: Dickens et al. (Cook AR senior author) · Lancet Regional Health Western Pacific 2020 · PMC7395828

text: The model has been previously used to estimate the effects of early epidemic control and of home versus institutional isolation of cases, and has been updated and expanded to assess exit strategies.
source: Dickens et al. (Cook AR senior author) · Lancet Regional Health Western Pacific 2020 · PMC7395828

text: In summary, we investigate the effects of early social distancing, lockdown and GRES over 480 days.
source: Dickens et al. (Cook AR senior author) · Lancet Regional Health Western Pacific 2020 · PMC7395828

text: Households were constructed using 178 census tables based on a sample of 200,000 households.
source: Dickens et al. (Cook AR senior author) · Lancet Regional Health Western Pacific 2020 · PMC7395828

text: An heuristic search algorithm was used to create a total of 3.77 million Singaporeans with the attributes of age, ethnicity and gender.
source: Dickens et al. (Cook AR senior author) · Lancet Regional Health Western Pacific 2020 · PMC7395828

text: Remaining attributes were drawn randomly from the specified attribute's marginal distribution and summary tables of the population comparable to the census tables formed whose fit were assessed using Pearson's chi-squared statistic.
source: Dickens et al. (Cook AR senior author) · Lancet Regional Health Western Pacific 2020 · PMC7395828

text: The same process was used to generate partners, allocate children and create multi-generational families for 1.14 million households.
source: Dickens et al. (Cook AR senior author) · Lancet Regional Health Western Pacific 2020 · PMC7395828

text: Individuals who were not working or studying were modelled to interact with people in the same residential community.
source: Dickens et al. (Cook AR senior author) · Lancet Regional Health Western Pacific 2020 · PMC7395828

text: The reproduction number was built with a multiplier gamma, which modified the infectiousness parameter of each individual in the simulation.
source: Dickens et al. (Cook AR senior author) · Lancet Regional Health Western Pacific 2020 · PMC7395828

text: We first simulate the initial 4 weeks for a selected gamma between 0 and 1.
source: Dickens et al. (Cook AR senior author) · Lancet Regional Health Western Pacific 2020 · PMC7395828

text: This value was used in the linearized form of the susceptible-exposed-infectious-removed (SEIR) model to compute the corresponding basic reproduction number.
source: Dickens et al. (Cook AR senior author) · Lancet Regional Health Western Pacific 2020 · PMC7395828

text: A grid search was performed on gamma, with the gamma that corresponded closest to a basic reproduction number of 2.0 being selected.
source: Dickens et al. (Cook AR senior author) · Lancet Regional Health Western Pacific 2020 · PMC7395828

text: For each scenario, we had case importation based on a Poisson model with lambda = 2.0.
source: Dickens et al. (Cook AR senior author) · Lancet Regional Health Western Pacific 2020 · PMC7395828

text: Our baseline scenario included the isolation of ascertained cases and home quarantine of their household members.
source: Dickens et al. (Cook AR senior author) · Lancet Regional Health Western Pacific 2020 · PMC7395828

text: We additionally assumed perfect compliance of those under household quarantine as strict punitive measures are in place.
source: Dickens et al. (Cook AR senior author) · Lancet Regional Health Western Pacific 2020 · PMC7395828

text: For the post lockdown strategy, two scenarios were modelled.
source: Dickens et al. (Cook AR senior author) · Lancet Regional Health Western Pacific 2020 · PMC7395828

text: The first assumed conditions went back to a pre-epidemic state with all schools, workplaces and the community at 100% transmission.
source: Dickens et al. (Cook AR senior author) · Lancet Regional Health Western Pacific 2020 · PMC7395828

text: The second, labelled as the gradual release exit strategy (GRES), assumed a successive restoration of contact rates over a period of three months.
source: Dickens et al. (Cook AR senior author) · Lancet Regional Health Western Pacific 2020 · PMC7395828

text: At a greater asymptomatic proportion of 44% we observed similar outcomes in terms of cumulative infection numbers for lockdown implementation on week 5 and 6 although it represented an overall accelerated epidemic.
source: Dickens et al. (Cook AR senior author) · Lancet Regional Health Western Pacific 2020 · PMC7395828

text: For a week 6 implementation time, 12.84% of cases can be averted with 8 weeks of social distancing relative to the baseline in comparison to 8 weeks of lockdown and GRES at 15.45%.
source: Dickens et al. (Cook AR senior author) · Lancet Regional Health Western Pacific 2020 · PMC7395828

text: Our findings suggest that earlier lockdown requires a GRES to prevent a large secondary peak, which becomes less important the later the lockdown is implemented.
source: Dickens et al. (Cook AR senior author) · Lancet Regional Health Western Pacific 2020 · PMC7395828

text: GRES therefore shows good utility in populations where substantial proportions are susceptible to infection, reducing the overall outbreak size and slowing down infection spread with a greater number of transmission events prevented.
source: Dickens et al. (Cook AR senior author) · Lancet Regional Health Western Pacific 2020 · PMC7395828

text: This is especially paramount as the number of cases beyond 365 days, although considerably lower than the initial peaks, still ranges from 6.51-513.21 cases per day for GRES strategies and 4.94-90.03 for long term social distancing strategies with the ongoing risk of secondary case spread from imported cases.
source: Dickens et al. (Cook AR senior author) · Lancet Regional Health Western Pacific 2020 · PMC7395828

text: At the start of the epidemic however, the duration of lockdown has a limited impact on the efficacy of GRES in terms of final infection attack size, which suggests that the period should be used for epidemic preparation rather than an ongoing control method, although an extended lockdown of 8 or 9 weeks will avert more cases.
source: Dickens et al. (Cook AR senior author) · Lancet Regional Health Western Pacific 2020 · PMC7395828

text: Should medical capacity permit, long term social distancing remains a viable strategy provided it is carried out for a duration of at least 6 weeks with 50% of the population working and schools closed.
source: Dickens et al. (Cook AR senior author) · Lancet Regional Health Western Pacific 2020 · PMC7395828

text: With GRES in place, which will still require healthcare system ramp-up, real-time forecasting efforts can also continue to estimate appropriate intervention trigger times should another lockdown be required.
source: Dickens et al. (Cook AR senior author) · Lancet Regional Health Western Pacific 2020 · PMC7395828

text: Additionally, containment measures and lockdowns vary widely in duration and severity between countries, causing differing and delayed epidemic peaks among source countries, making lockdown a temporary protection measure against highly uncertain external epidemiological forces where delays in reactive control measures abroad or within Singapore will result in inevitable national case spread.
source: Dickens et al. (Cook AR senior author) · Lancet Regional Health Western Pacific 2020 · PMC7395828

text: Limitations of this study include uncertainties on the current number of infections, which could not be used directly to validate the initial phase of the epidemic in the agent-based model.
source: Dickens et al. (Cook AR senior author) · Lancet Regional Health Western Pacific 2020 · PMC7395828

text: The model can be calibrated in the future with real time forecasting efforts and results of serology surveys to better reflect COVID-19 prevalence and incidence within Singapore.
source: Dickens et al. (Cook AR senior author) · Lancet Regional Health Western Pacific 2020 · PMC7395828

text: Further uncertainties include the current and future adherence to social distancing measures, future importation rates and spatial heterogeneities in infection rates.
source: Dickens et al. (Cook AR senior author) · Lancet Regional Health Western Pacific 2020 · PMC7395828

text: Abstract A novel coronavirus disease (COVID-19) outbreak has now spread to a number of countries worldwide.
source: Endo et al. · Wellcome Open Research 2020 · PMC7338915

text: We quantified individual-level variation in COVID-19 transmission by applying a mathematical model to observed outbreak sizes in affected countries.
source: Endo et al. · Wellcome Open Research 2020 · PMC7338915

text: We extracted the number of imported and local cases in the affected countries from the World Health Organization situation report and applied a branching process model where the number of secondary transmissions was assumed to follow a negative-binomial distribution.
source: Endo et al. · Wellcome Open Research 2020 · PMC7338915

text: Our finding of a highly-overdispersed offspring distribution highlights a potential benefit to focusing intervention efforts on superspreading.
source: Endo et al. · Wellcome Open Research 2020 · PMC7338915

text: As most infected individuals do not contribute to the expansion of an epidemic, the effective reproduction number could be drastically reduced by preventing relatively rare superspreading events.

text: Introduction A novel coronavirus disease (COVID-19) outbreak, which is considered to be associated with a market in Wuhan, China, is now affecting a number of countries worldwide.
source: Endo et al. · Wellcome Open Research 2020 · PMC7338915

text: More than 100 countries have observed confirmed cases of COVID-19.
source: Endo et al. · Wellcome Open Research 2020 · PMC7338915

text: A few countries have already been shifting from the containment phase to the mitigation phase, with a substantial number of locally acquired cases (including those whose epidemiological link is untraceable).
source: Endo et al. · Wellcome Open Research 2020 · PMC7338915

text: We estimated the level of overdispersion in COVID-19 transmission by using a mathematical model that is characterised by and the overdispersion parameter of a negative binomial branching process.
source: Endo et al. · Wellcome Open Research 2020 · PMC7338915

text: To distinguish between countries with and without an ongoing outbreak, we extracted daily case counts from an online resource and determined the dates of the latest case confirmation for each country (as of 27 February).
source: Endo et al. · Wellcome Open Research 2020 · PMC7338915

text: Assuming that the offspring distributions (distribution of the number of secondary transmissions) for COVID-19 cases are identically- and independently-distributed negative-binomial distributions, we constructed the likelihood of observing the reported number of imported/local cases (outbreak size) of COVID-19 for each country.
source: Endo et al. · Wellcome Open Research 2020 · PMC7338915

text: If the observed case counts are part of an ongoing outbreak in a country, cluster sizes may grow in the future.
source: Endo et al. · Wellcome Open Research 2020 · PMC7338915

text: To address this issue, we adjusted the likelihood for those countries with ongoing outbreak by only using the condition that the final cluster size of such a country has to be larger than the currently observed number of cases.
source: Endo et al. · Wellcome Open Research 2020 · PMC7338915

text: We applied the final size likelihood to those countries and the alternative to the rest of the countries (countries with an ongoing outbreak).
source: Endo et al. · Wellcome Open Research 2020 · PMC7338915

text: Varying the assumed between 0-5 (fixed at an evenly-spaced grid of values), we estimated the overdispersion parameter using the likelihood function described above.
source: Endo et al. · Wellcome Open Research 2020 · PMC7338915

text: We used the Markov-chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) method to provide 95% credible intervals (CrIs).
source: Endo et al. · Wellcome Open Research 2020 · PMC7338915

text: We also performed a joint-estimation of and by the MCMC method (with a weakly-informed normal prior for and the weakly-informed half-normal prior for the reciprocal of).
source: Endo et al. · Wellcome Open Research 2020 · PMC7338915

text: We compared the two models by the widely-applicable Bayesian information criterion (WBIC).
source: Endo et al. · Wellcome Open Research 2020 · PMC7338915

text: We used simulations to investigate potential bias caused by underreporting, one of the major limitations of the present study.
source: Endo et al. · Wellcome Open Research 2020 · PMC7338915

text: For the values of 2-3, the estimates suggested that 80% of secondary transmissions may have been caused by a small fraction of infectious individuals (~10%).
source: Endo et al. · Wellcome Open Research 2020 · PMC7338915

text: A scatterplot exhibited a moderate correlation between and (correlation coefficient -0.4).
source: Endo et al. · Wellcome Open Research 2020 · PMC7338915

text: Model comparison between negative-binomial and Poisson branching process models suggested that a negative-binomial model better describes the observed data; WBIC strongly supported the negative-binomial model with a difference of 11.0.
source: Endo et al. · Wellcome Open Research 2020 · PMC7338915

text: For the likely range of of 2-3, the overdispersion parameter was estimated to be around 0.1, suggesting that the majority of secondary transmission may be caused by a very small fraction of individuals (80% of transmissions caused by ~10% of the total cases).
source: Endo et al. · Wellcome Open Research 2020 · PMC7338915

text: These results are consistent with a number of observed superspreading events observed in the current COVID-19 outbreak, and also in line with the estimates from the previous SARS/MERS outbreaks.
source: Endo et al. · Wellcome Open Research 2020 · PMC7338915

text: The former study did not yield an interpretable estimate of due to the limited data input.

source: Endo et al. · Wellcome Open Research 2020 · PMC7338915

text: Although cluster size distributions based on a branching process model are useful in inference of the offspring distribution from limited data, they are not directly applicable to an ongoing outbreak because the final cluster size may not yet have been observed.
source: Endo et al. · Wellcome Open Research 2020 · PMC7338915

text: Even though we used the case counts in those countries only as the lower bounds of future final cluster sizes, which might have only partially informed of the underlying branching process, our model yielded estimates with moderate uncertainty levels (at least sufficient to suggest that may be below 1).
source: Endo et al. · Wellcome Open Research 2020 · PMC7338915

text: Together with the previous finding suggesting that the overdispersion parameter is unlikely to be biased downwards, we believe our analysis supports the possibility of highly-overdispersed transmission of COVID-19.
source: Endo et al. · Wellcome Open Research 2020 · PMC7338915

text: Reported cases whose site of infection classified as unknown, which should in principle be counted as either imported or local cases, were excluded from analysis.

text: However, we believe that our conclusion is robust because the distinction does not change with different thresholds (4-14 days), within which the serial interval of SARS-CoV-2 is likely to fall.

text: Abstract Regional monitoring of the proportion of the population who have been infected by SARS-CoV-2 is important to guide local management of the epidemic, but is difficult in the absence of regular nationwide serosurveys.
source: Hozé et al. · Lancet Public Health 2021 · PMC8032222

text: We aimed to estimate in near real time the proportion of adults who have been infected by SARS-CoV-2.
source: Hozé et al. · Lancet Public Health 2021 · PMC8032222

text: In this modelling study, we developed a method to reconstruct the proportion of adults who have been infected by SARS-CoV-2 and the proportion of infections being detected, using the joint analysis of age-stratified seroprevalence, hospitalisation, and case data, with deconvolution methods.
source: Hozé et al. · Lancet Public Health 2021 · PMC8032222

text: We developed our method on a dataset consisting of seroprevalence estimates from 9782 participants (aged >=20 years) in the two worst affected regions of France in May, 2020, and applied our approach to the 13 French metropolitan regions over the period March, 2020, to January, 2021.
source: Hozé et al. · Lancet Public Health 2021 · PMC8032222

text: Our regional estimates of seroprevalence were strongly correlated with the external validation dataset (coefficient of correlation 0.89).
source: Hozé et al. · Lancet Public Health 2021 · PMC8032222

text: This information will become ever more important as the epidemic progresses and spatial heterogeneities in population immunity potentially increase.
source: Hozé et al. · Lancet Public Health 2021 · PMC8032222

text: Unfortunately, up-to-date estimates of seroprevalence able to capture the most recent regional evolution of the epidemic are unavailable.
source: Hozé et al. · Lancet Public Health 2021 · PMC8032222

text: It is therefore important to develop methods that can track the proportion of the population that has been infected in different regions using the joint analysis of existing seroprevalence data and other surveillance data that are more readily available in real time.
source: Hozé et al. · Lancet Public Health 2021 · PMC8032222

text: However, such an approach might have difficulties in capturing spread in younger age groups given low infection-fatality ratios in these groups, and might provide lagged estimates given the relatively long delays between infection and death.
source: Hozé et al. · Lancet Public Health 2021 · PMC8032222

text: Here, we present a method to reconstruct the proportion of the adult population infected by SARS-CoV-2 and the proportion of infections detected by surveillance from the joint analysis of age-stratified seroprevalence, hospitalisation, and case data.
source: Hozé et al. · Lancet Public Health 2021 · PMC8032222

text: 9782 adult participants (aged >=20 years) were recruited in the SAPRIS study in Île-de-France and Grand Est and sampling weights were used to adjust for selection and participation in the cohorts before random selection.
source: Hozé et al. · Lancet Public Health 2021 · PMC8032222

text: Sociodemographic covariates were used to correct for selection and participation bias.
source: Hozé et al. · Lancet Public Health 2021 · PMC8032222

text: Seroprevalence status of the participants was inferred using a series of tests (ELISA-S, ELISA-NP, and seroneutralisation).
source: Hozé et al. · Lancet Public Health 2021 · PMC8032222

text: The serological status of those remaining participants was inferred using a multiple imputation method.
source: Hozé et al. · Lancet Public Health 2021 · PMC8032222

text: For each age group, the number of infections was obtained as the deconvolution of the daily number of hospitalisations and the infection-to-hospitalisation delay distribution, divided by the IHR.
source: Hozé et al. · Lancet Public Health 2021 · PMC8032222

text: The heterogeneity of infections across regions was assessed using the coefficient of variation (CV).
source: Hozé et al. · Lancet Public Health 2021 · PMC8032222

text: We validated our method externally using a separate national seroprevalence study done between May 2 and June 2, 2020, among individuals aged 15 years or older in 12 regions of metropolitan France.
source: Hozé et al. · Lancet Public Health 2021 · PMC8032222

text: Pearson's correlation was used to compare seroprevalence estimated with the model and from the external dataset.
source: Hozé et al. · Lancet Public Health 2021 · PMC8032222

text: Dates of infections of confirmed cases were reconstructed with the same deconvolution approach using the national virological surveillance database of confirmed cases (SI-DEP) and assuming the infection-to-detection delay has a gamma distribution of mean 8.5 days and SD 2.8 days, which accounts for an incubation period of 5.5 days and a delay of 3 days to testing.
source: Hozé et al. · Lancet Public Health 2021 · PMC8032222

text: Proportions of infections detected by surveillance were estimated over three periods (June 1 to Aug 31, 2020; Sept 1 to Oct 31, 2020; and Nov 1, 2020 to Jan 15, 2021) for all 13 regions as the ratio of the cumulative number of infections reconstructed from the confirmed cases recorded in SI-DEP over the cumulative number of infections, as estimated with the hospitalisation data.
source: Hozé et al. · Lancet Public Health 2021 · PMC8032222

text: We studied the impact of the delay distributions on the estimated proportion of infected individuals in the population and on the proportion of cases detected.
source: Hozé et al. · Lancet Public Health 2021 · PMC8032222

text: We changed the mean and variance of the gamma distribution of the time-to-hospitalisation delay, and varied the delay with age and over the course of the epidemic.
source: Hozé et al. · Lancet Public Health 2021 · PMC8032222

text: Finally, we evaluated the impact of a 10-30% decrease of the IHR during the second wave.
source: Hozé et al. · Lancet Public Health 2021 · PMC8032222

text: The patterns of hospitalisations by age and the IHR were similar in Grand Est and Île-de-France.
source: Hozé et al. · Lancet Public Health 2021 · PMC8032222

text: Our regional estimates of seroprevalence in May were strongly correlated with the external validation dataset (coefficient of correlation 0.89), with ten of the 12 estimates contained in the 95% CI of the serosurvey.
source: Hozé et al. · Lancet Public Health 2021 · PMC8032222

text: These estimates are consistent with a simple analysis of the raw data from the SI-VIC and SI-DEP databases: between June 1 and Nov 30, 2020, approximately 170 000 adults were hospitalised and 2 400 000 cases were detected by surveillance in metropolitan France, leading to a proportion detected of about 46% for an average estimated IHR of 3.3%.
source: Hozé et al. · Lancet Public Health 2021 · PMC8032222

text: We therefore conducted a series of sensitivity analyses and showed that our results on the proportion infected and proportion detected were robust to misspecification of the delay distributions.
source: Hozé et al. · Lancet Public Health 2021 · PMC8032222

text: Discussion We have presented a method to reconstruct the proportion of the adult population infected by SARS-CoV-2 by region and age group from the joint analysis of readily available hospital surveillance data and existing serological surveys.
source: Hozé et al. · Lancet Public Health 2021 · PMC8032222

text: This approach offers a simple way to track the number of infections in the population with a lag of a few weeks (ie, from infection to hospitalisation), which is challenging in the absence of regular, large-scale, representative serosurveys.
source: Hozé et al. · Lancet Public Health 2021 · PMC8032222

text: After accounting for the imperfect sensitivity of serology, we estimate that the proportion infected by SARS-CoV-2 in metropolitan France increased by two to three times from about 6% in May, 2020, to about 15% in mid-January, 2021.
source: Hozé et al. · Lancet Public Health 2021 · PMC8032222

text: Second, while the first wave was mostly concentrated in two regions, all regions were impacted by the second wave.
source: Hozé et al. · Lancet Public Health 2021 · PMC8032222

text: This does not take into account the potential waning of natural immunity.
source: Hozé et al. · Lancet Public Health 2021 · PMC8032222

text: First, although most people infected by SARS-CoV-2 appear to acquire protection against reinfection for at least 6 months, we still lack data to document waning of immunity over longer time periods.
source: Hozé et al. · Lancet Public Health 2021 · PMC8032222

text: Obviously, as the vaccine roll-out progresses, it will be essential to track the level of immunity acquired through vaccination.
source: Hozé et al. · Lancet Public Health 2021 · PMC8032222

text: As more recent seroprevalence studies and data on the duration of immunity become available, this information could easily be integrated into our statistical framework to estimate the proportion of the population that is currently immunised.
source: Hozé et al. · Lancet Public Health 2021 · PMC8032222

text: In a sensitivity analysis, assuming a reduced IHR during the second wave had little impact on the proportion infected.
source: Hozé et al. · Lancet Public Health 2021 · PMC8032222

text: However, despite these possible regional and contextual variations in IHRs, our regional estimates of seroprevalence were strongly correlated with our external validation dataset, despite using IHR estimates only for Île-de-France and Grand Est, the two regions that were the most affected during the first wave.
source: Hozé et al. · Lancet Public Health 2021 · PMC8032222

text: Our results should be robust to variations in the age distribution of those infected since our approach controls for age.
source: Hozé et al. · Lancet Public Health 2021 · PMC8032222

text: In conclusion, we have presented a simple framework to track the proportion of the population infected with a lag of a few weeks using the joint analysis of age-stratified hospitalisation and serological data.
source: Hozé et al. · Lancet Public Health 2021 · PMC8032222

text: Age-specific IHRs might vary by country given the different health-care systems.
source: Hozé et al. · Lancet Public Health 2021 · PMC8032222

text: However, it should be easy to recalibrate our model to data from countries in which hospital surveillance and results of serosurveys are available.
source: Hozé et al. · Lancet Public Health 2021 · PMC8032222

text: Abstract As SARS-CoV-2 continues to spread, a thorough characterisation of healthcare needs and patient outcomes, and how they have changed over time, is essential to inform planning.
source: Lefrancq et al. · Lancet Regional Health Europe 2021 · PMC7981225

text: We found that there were marked changes in the age and sex of hospitalisations over the study period.
source: Lefrancq et al. · Lancet Regional Health Europe 2021 · PMC7981225

text: In particular, the proportion of hospitalised individuals that were >80y varied between 27% and 48% over the course of the epidemic, and was lowest during the inter-peak period.
source: Lefrancq et al. · Lancet Regional Health Europe 2021 · PMC7981225

text: Overall, we find both the probability of death and the probability of entering ICU were significantly correlated with COVID-19 ICU occupancy.
source: Lefrancq et al. · Lancet Regional Health Europe 2021 · PMC7981225

text: These need to be considered in ongoing healthcare planning efforts.
source: Lefrancq et al. · Lancet Regional Health Europe 2021 · PMC7981225

text: Introduction The rapid nature of the severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) spread placed unprecedented strain on healthcare facilities around the world.
source: Lefrancq et al. · Lancet Regional Health Europe 2021 · PMC7981225

text: Accurate projections of healthcare needs can help plan the pressure on the healthcare system, try to prevent them from reaching capacity and ensure they are well equipped to deal with increasing demand.
source: Lefrancq et al. · Lancet Regional Health Europe 2021 · PMC7981225

text: Finally, improvements in clinical care may also have modified outcomes as clinicians progressively learned to manage COVID-19 patients, including through new treatment strategies.
source: Lefrancq et al. · Lancet Regional Health Europe 2021 · PMC7981225

text: More recently, studies have shown substantial improvement in hospital mortality over the first epidemic wave in the UK and in the US.
source: Lefrancq et al. · Lancet Regional Health Europe 2021 · PMC7981225

text: Here, we aim to shed a new light on the evolution of in-hospital mortality through the analysis of 9 months of data, which include the first and second 2020 epidemic wave in France.
source: Lefrancq et al. · Lancet Regional Health Europe 2021 · PMC7981225

text: Using data from a dedicated COVID-19 surveillance system that was rapidly integrated into all French hospitals, we characterise the complex hospital pathways of COVID-19 patients.
source: Lefrancq et al. · Lancet Regional Health Europe 2021 · PMC7981225

text: The study also provides a detailed account of the way the French healthcare system coped with an unprecedented wave of hospitalisations during this unique crisis in French history.
source: Lefrancq et al. · Lancet Regional Health Europe 2021 · PMC7981225

text: Methods We used a linelist of hospitalised patients from the SI-VIC database who started their hospitalisation between 13 March and 30 November 2020.
source: Lefrancq et al. · Lancet Regional Health Europe 2021 · PMC7981225

text: We worked on an anonymized version of the dataset, with each patient having only an ID number.
source: Lefrancq et al. · Lancet Regional Health Europe 2021 · PMC7981225

text: We consider that all patients are initially admitted to hospital.
source: Lefrancq et al. · Lancet Regional Health Europe 2021 · PMC7981225

text: In initial analyses, we found that the delays from hospitalisation to ICU admission or death did not differ substantially by age and sex, and so we used a single delay distribution from hospitalisation to ICU, and one delay distribution from hospitalisation to death across all individuals (irrespective of age or sex).
source: Lefrancq et al. · Lancet Regional Health Europe 2021 · PMC7981225

text: We modelled the delay from hospitalisation to ICU using a zero-inflated exponential distribution.
source: Lefrancq et al. · Lancet Regional Health Europe 2021 · PMC7981225

text: The delays from ICU to death and hospital discharge were modelled using a lognormal distribution.
source: Lefrancq et al. · Lancet Regional Health Europe 2021 · PMC7981225

text: We also considered a gamma distribution as a sensitivity analysis.
source: Lefrancq et al. · Lancet Regional Health Europe 2021 · PMC7981225

text: We used a probabilistic framework based on competing risk models with cause-specific relative hazards.
source: Lefrancq et al. · Lancet Regional Health Europe 2021 · PMC7981225

text: We used the percentage of ICU occupancy by COVID-19 patients as a proxy to monitor the pressure on the healthcare system.
source: Lefrancq et al. · Lancet Regional Health Europe 2021 · PMC7981225

text: We assessed the performance of the model on both a fixed and a varying risk over time, as well as a fixed and a varying delay from admission to death.
source: Lefrancq et al. · Lancet Regional Health Europe 2021 · PMC7981225

text: Seventy three percent of the deaths among patients that did not enter ICU were aged >80y, whereas only 24% of deaths among those admitted to ICU were in the oldest age group.
source: Lefrancq et al. · Lancet Regional Health Europe 2021 · PMC7981225

text: In particular, the proportion of hospitalised individuals that were >80y varied between 27% during the summer 2020 and 48% at the peak of the first wave.
source: Lefrancq et al. · Lancet Regional Health Europe 2021 · PMC7981225

text: The proportion of hospitalised cases that were female increased from 45% to 53% during the spring before returning to 48% by the end of November.
source: Lefrancq et al. · Lancet Regional Health Europe 2021 · PMC7981225

text: The age and sex distribution of those entering ICU also changed, contrasting with those that died, which remained approximately stable.
source: Lefrancq et al. · Lancet Regional Health Europe 2021 · PMC7981225

Discussion Experiences across the globe to date have highlighted the significant public health threat that new SARS-CoV-2 VOCs can pose, even in settings where transmission is currently under control or where population-level immunity should preclude resurgence.

Variants under investigation such as B.1.525 and A.23.1 have undergone periods of rapid expansion in January-March 2021 associated with travel-related importation and limited local spread, only to subside later.
While >20% of sequenced cases were from non-B.1.1.7 lineages as of mid-April, the fraction was only around 10% in cases not known to be associated with travel or surge testing.

While the ONS Infection Survey did not show signs of an increase in S+ in April (probably because the overall number of positive cases was very low), this population survey shows a marked increase in S+ in May, matching the other data streams.
Finally, wastewater surveillance for North London is consistent with the rapid emergence of B.1.617.2 in April/May.

Several studies suggest that VOCs B.1.1.7, P.1, B.1.351, and B.1.617.2 are more transmissible than previously circulating lineages, but precise estimates of their relative transmissibility are not yet available.

Our results underscore the value of utilising a diverse array of data sources in community surveillance.

Such information is critical to the epidemic's immediate control and to future vaccine development and deployment - both in the UK and other countries where the potential emergence of other novel SARS-CoV-2 variants remains a serious public health threat.
